name: Vivah Panchami in Janakpur
when: Nov–Dec, Mangsir Shukla Panchami; 14 December in 2026
summary: Vivah Panchami celebrates the wedding of Sita and Rama on the fifth day of the bright half of Mangsir. In Janakpur, Sita's city, it is the biggest festival of the year, with a week of processions, Ramayana recitals and a full re-enactment of the wedding at the Janaki Mandir and Vivah Mandap.
body: Hindus believe Rama and Sita married in Janakpur after Rama broke Shiva's bow at Sita's swayamvara. Vivah Panchami marks that wedding on Margashirsha (Mangsir) Shukla Panchami, which falls in late November or December. In 2026 it falls on Monday 14 December by most published calendars; dates follow the lunar calendar, so check current status before you travel. Celebrations in Janakpur build for about a week beforehand, with daily kirtan, Ramlila performances and readings from the Ramcharitmanas.

The key events follow the stages of a Hindu wedding. A barat, the groom's procession, carries images of Rama through the streets on decorated chariots and floats, with bands, flags and thousands of devotees. Pilgrims from Ayodhya often arrive with a procession of their own, honouring the link between Rama's city and Sita's. On the wedding day, priests perform the rites at the Vivah Mandap beside the Janaki Mandir, including the tilak, kanyadan and the circling of the sacred fire.

For visitors it is the best and hardest time to see Janakpur. The city is full, hotels sell out weeks in advance and prices rise, the main lanes are packed from morning to night, and temple queues are long. The reward is a living religious drama, enacted by a whole city. Our Vivah Panchami tour books rooms near the temple months ahead and uses a local guide to manage timings and crowds.
tips: Book flights and hotels at least two months ahead; Janakpur has limited rooms and they fill fast.
Stay within walking distance of the Janaki Mandir, as roads close to vehicles during processions.
Agree a fixed meeting point with your group each day; phone networks get congested in the crowds.
Mid-December nights in Janakpur can fall to 8–10 °C with fog, so bring a warm layer.
Keep valuables to a minimum and wear shoes that are easy to remove for temple visits.

faqs.a: Vivah Panchami falls on Margashirsha Shukla Panchami. In 2026 most published calendars give Monday 14 December, with the panchami tithi starting on the afternoon of 13 December. Celebrations in Janakpur run for about a week before. Lunar dates can differ slightly between calendars, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What happens at Vivah Panchami in Janakpur?
faqs.a: A week of Ramayana readings, kirtan and Ramlila leads up to the festival. Rama's wedding procession travels through the city with chariots and bands, often joined by pilgrims from Ayodhya, and on the main day priests re-enact the wedding rites at the Vivah Mandap beside the Janaki Mandir, watched by huge crowds.

faqs.q: How crowded is Janakpur during Vivah Panchami?
faqs.a: Very crowded. Pilgrims arrive from across Nepal and India, and the area around the Janaki Mandir is packed for several days. Hotels sell out and roads close. It is manageable with a guide, a hotel close to the temple and patience. Seniors should plan rest breaks away from the main lanes.

faqs.q: Can I attend the Sita–Ram wedding ceremony as a visitor?
faqs.a: Yes. The procession and the ceremonies at the Vivah Mandap are public, and visitors of all faiths are welcome to watch respectfully. Space near the pavilion is limited, so arrive early. Dress modestly, remove shoes in temple areas and ask before photographing priests or families.

name: Chitwan Elephant and Tourism Festival
when: Late December, usually three days (26–28 December in 2025)
summary: Held in Sauraha since the late 1990s, this three-day festival features an elephant parade, elephant football and races, Tharu dances and the ritual worship of elephants. It draws large domestic crowds. We describe it honestly, including the welfare concerns animal groups raise about such events.
body: The Chitwan Elephant and Tourism Festival is organised by the Regional Hotel Association of Chitwan with the local elephant owners' cooperative, to promote tourism in Sauraha and celebrate the role of elephants in the area. The 19th edition ran from 26 to 28 December 2025 at the Baghmara community forest grounds, with around 80 elephants taking part. Dates are set each year by the organisers, so check current status before you travel.

The programme mixes Tharu culture with elephant events. A parade of painted elephants opens the festival, followed over three days by elephant races, elephant football, an elephant beauty contest, Tharu stick and peacock dances, music and food stalls. The last day traditionally includes the worship of the elephants and an elephant picnic, when the animals are fed large meals of fruit, rice and molasses. Crowds are mostly Nepali and Indian holidaymakers.

We think travellers should know the other side too. Animal-welfare organisations have criticised races, football and the training that makes such displays possible, and they argue that captive elephants are best kept away from crowds and performance. Some visitors enjoy the parade and Tharu dances and skip the contests. We do not sell elephant rides at any time of year, and if you visit Sauraha during the festival we will plan your safaris around it and let you choose which parts, if any, to attend.
tips: Book Sauraha hotels early; the festival overlaps with the Indian winter holidays and Christmas.
Watch the parade and Tharu dances from a distance and leave the crowded contest areas to others if you prefer.
Keep well back from the elephants, which can be stressed by crowds and noise.
Late-December mornings are foggy and cold, around 7–10 °C, so plan safaris for later in the morning.
Read up on captive-elephant welfare before deciding whether to attend; we are happy to talk it through.

faqs.q: Is the Chitwan Elephant Festival still held?
faqs.a: Yes. The 19th Elephant and Tourism Festival took place in Sauraha from 26 to 28 December 2025, with around 80 elephants. It has been held regularly since the late 1990s, though dates and programmes change. Check current status before you travel, as the organisers announce dates each autumn.

faqs.q: What happens at the Sauraha elephant festival?
faqs.a: An elephant parade, elephant races and football, an elephant beauty contest, Tharu cultural dances, music, food stalls and, on the final day, the worship of the elephants followed by an elephant picnic of fruit and rice. Events take place at the Baghmara community forest grounds near Sauraha.

It is debated. Organisers present it as celebrating elephants and Tharu culture. Animal-welfare groups criticise races, football and the training behind them. We do not sell elephant rides and leave it to each traveller to decide whether to attend, with honest information. Many people watch only the parade and dances.

faqs.q: Can I combine the elephant festival with a safari?
faqs.a: Yes. The festival runs alongside normal park activities, so you can do jeep, canoe and walking safaris in the mornings and see parts of the festival in the afternoons. Hotels are busy, so book early. Late December is cool and foggy, with good wildlife viewing later in the morning.
